historical_timeline.summary: His father changed both their names to Martin Luther after a journey to Berlin.
Death of his grandmother; an impulsive act of self-injury in grief, at twelve.
Doctorate from Boston University, after Morehouse and Crozer.
His home in Montgomery was bombed.
Stabbed in the chest in Harlem; thoracic surgery at Harlem Hospital.
Arrests and jailings in Atlanta, Albany and Birmingham.
FBI wiretaps on his home and offices authorized; surveillance continued.
In St. Joseph's Infirmary for exhaustion and a respiratory infection when the Nobel Peace Prize was announced.
The FBI anonymously sent him a recording and a letter.
Received the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.
Led the march from Selma to Montgomery.
A heavy smoker who hid his cigarettes; depression described by biographers.
People close to him tried to arrange mental health care; he refused.
Assassinated in Memphis; buried in Atlanta on April 9.

claims.statement: He was born Michael King on January 15, 1929, at 501 Auburn Avenue in Atlanta, Georgia.

In 1934 his father, the Reverend Michael King, attended the Baptist World Alliance meeting in Berlin and afterwards changed his own name and his son's from Michael to Martin Luther, after the German Protestant reformer; the son's birth certificate was altered to read Martin Luther King, Jr. on July 23, 1957.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Explains his name; the reformer Martin Luther has his own record (HR-RE004). Context only.

source_links.locator: after the German Protestant leader; birth certificate altered July 23, 1957

claims.statement: His grandmother, Jennie Celeste Williams, died on May 18, 1941, when he was twelve, while he was at a parade without his parents' permission. Grieved and remorseful, he reacted with an impulsive act of self-injury at home. The editors of his papers note that neither he nor his father later described this as a suicide attempt; his father wrote that he cried off and on for several days and could not sleep at night.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A documented act of self-injury in childhood grief. The roster's 'suicide attempt at 12' overstates the sources and is not adopted. Recorded once; the modern record refers to it only as an impulsive act of self-injury in grief.

source_links.locator: Introduction: 18 May 1941; impulsive reaction; neither mentioned a suicide attempt

claims.statement: He entered Morehouse College in 1944, was ordained in 1948, graduated from Crozer Theological Seminary in 1951, and received his doctorate in systematic theology from Boston University on June 5, 1955.
He married Coretta Scott on June 18, 1953, at the Scott home near Marion, Alabama.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context; no health fact, statement or decision of his wife or children is used in the modern episode.

claims.statement: As president of the Montgomery Improvement Association during the bus boycott, his home was bombed on the evening of January 30, 1956, while he spoke at a mass meeting; his wife and daughter were not hurt, and he pleaded with an angry crowd for nonviolence.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented violent threat to his family.

claims.statement: On September 20, 1958, at a book signing at Blumstein's Department Store in Harlem, he was stabbed in the upper left side of the chest with a seven-inch steel letter opener. At Harlem Hospital he had more than two hours of surgery; the blade lay so close to the aorta that, he was told, a sneeze could have punctured it, and he wrote that his whole chest had to be opened to remove it. He left the hospital on October 3 and convalesced until late October.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented chest wound and thoracic surgery; anchors the old scar and the trauma history in the modern episode.

source_links.locator: 20 September 1958; seven-inch letter opener; more than two hours of surgery; aorta
my whole chest had to be opened; released October 3

claims.statement: He was arrested and jailed repeatedly: at a sit-in at Rich's department store in Atlanta in October 1960, when he was sentenced to four months of hard labor for violating probation; in Albany, Georgia, in December 1961 and in July 1962, when he spent two weeks in jail; and in Birmingham from April 12 to 19, 1963.

The FBI monitored him from December 1955; wiretaps on his home and the SCLC offices were authorized in October 1963, and he was subjected to surveillance under the counterintelligence program. In about November 1964 the FBI anonymously sent him a recording with an anonymous letter that SCLC staff read as urging him to take his own life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented surveillance and the anonymous letter. Its content is not quoted. Anchors the threat and privacy concerns in the modern episode.

claims.statement: In October 1964, exhausted by a heavy speaking schedule and with a respiratory infection, he was admitted to St. Joseph's Infirmary in Atlanta for several days of rest; he was asleep there on October 14, 1964, when his wife telephoned to tell him he had been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented admission for exhaustion; the brief's 'viral infection' is recorded as a respiratory infection, as the source says. Anchors the presenting exhaustion.

source_links.locator: Exhausted by a heavy speaking schedule and suffering from a respiratory infection
sleeping in an Atlanta hospital room after checking in for a rest

claims.statement: He received the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo on December 10, 1964, at 35 the youngest person to have won it.
After voting rights marchers were beaten at the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma on March 7, 1965, he led the march from Selma to Montgomery from March 17 to 25, 1965.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context: the sustained campaign just before the index date.

claims.statement: A man who drove for the King family in the mid-1960s described him as a chain smoker who kept his cigarettes hidden at home.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A first-hand account in a national public radio report; anchors the modern tobacco use. The driver is not named here.

source_links.locator: Dr. King was a chain smoker

claims.statement: Biographers and historians describe depression in his adult life: David Garrow wrote that, partly as a result of the FBI's intimidation, he often suffered from morbid depression, a contention others have disputed; a psychologist writing in 2024 states that, although never diagnosed, he had serious bouts of depression that he kept secret for fear it could be used against him.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective and secondhand; no historical psychiatric diagnosis is adopted. Anchors the synthetic modern depression and the privacy concern.

never officially diagnosed; fear it could be used against him

claims.statement: According to the historian Taylor Branch, as reported in a newspaper caption, his autopsy showed the heart of a 60-year-old man, which Branch attributed to stress.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Reported secondhand; the autopsy report was not seen. After the index date; history only.

claims.statement: On April 4, 1968, he was shot and killed while standing on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, where he had come to support striking sanitation workers; he was buried in Atlanta on April 9.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; history only.

claims.statement: The same 2024 commentary states that shortly before his death several people close to him tried to arrange mental health care for him, which he refused.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; history only.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Caring for a 36-year-old Black minister and public leader with exhaustion, insomnia and low mood under sustained, real threat: distinguishing major depressive disorder from an adjustment disorder by DSM-5-TR, and realistic vigilance from PTSD (PC-PTSD-5 and interview); a structured safety assessment that separates the expectation of being killed from suicidal ideation and weighs a childhood act of self-injury and a letter urging suicide; CBT, CBT for insomnia and sertraline by shared decision under the APA 1958 guideline and the ACP insomnia guideline; tobacco cessation with counseling and varenicline under the USPSTF 1960 recommendation and the EAGLES trial; confirming stage 1 hypertension with home readings and lifestyle treatment under the 1956 ACC/AHA guideline; lipids and risk at 36; an old thoracotomy scar; a sustainable work plan; and equity in care: racism and threat as causes of stress, trust and privacy for a patient under surveillance, and culturally responsive therapy that respects his faith.

documentation.chief_complaint: Two-week review of exhaustion, poor sleep and low mood, seen the same day in psychiatry

hpi.narrative: Dr. King returns two weeks after his first visit, on the day of his consultation with Dr. Lindqvist-Bankole. He has kept a sleep diary: he goes to bed after one in the morning, lies awake for an hour, wakes before five and cannot return to sleep, averaging about five hours. He feels low and flat most days, has lost his pleasure in reading and preaching, feels guilty that he cannot do more, and has trouble concentrating on his writing. He has more energy on the platform than anywhere else. He is always alert to danger in crowds and at home, but has no nightmares about the stabbing and does not avoid crowds or reminders. He has never had a period of days of high energy with little need for sleep. He has no thoughts of ending his life, although he often thinks he may be killed. He has not cut down his smoking.

assessment_plan.display: Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate
assessment_plan.assessment: The presenting exhaustion, poor sleep and low mood now have their diagnosis. referral.question: Exhaustion, broken sleep and low mood for about two months in a 36-year-old minister and civil rights leader who lives under sustained, real threat and works without rest. Please confirm the diagnosis (depression, an adjustment disorder, PTSD or an insomnia disorder), review his safety, and advise on therapy and medicine in a way that protects his privacy
referral.pertinent_history: Admitted for several days' rest for exhaustion and a respiratory infection six months ago. Since then he has worked without a break, sleeps about five hours, and feels drained, low and joyless. His home was bombed nine years ago; he was stabbed in the chest seven years ago and needed thoracic surgery; he has been jailed repeatedly; he receives threats by telephone and mail, including an anonymous letter urging him to end his life, and believes his calls are monitored. At twelve, in grief after his grandmother's death, he impulsively injured himself; he has not described it as a suicide attempt. PHQ-9 17 with item 9 scored 0; GAD-7 11; PC-PTSD-5 2; AUDIT-C 2. No suicidal ideation, intent or plan; he expects he may be killed but does not wish to die; safety plan made, with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Smokes about a pack a day. Blood pressure 138/88, home readings planned. Blood count, metabolic panel, TSH and hemoglobin A1c normal; LDL 142 mg/dL; ECG normal. No medicines; no known allergies. He is worried that a psychiatric record could be used against him and the movement; his chart is restricted
questions: Does he have major depressive disorder, an adjustment disorder, or another condition?
Does he have PTSD, given the stabbing, the bombing and the continuing threats, or is his vigilance proportionate to real danger?
How should his suicide risk be understood, given the childhood act of self-injury, the anonymous letter and his expectation of being killed?
What treatment do you recommend: psychotherapy, an antidepressant, or both, and how should his insomnia be treated?
Is varenicline safe for him to stop smoking alongside treatment for depression, and when should it start?
How can his care respect his faith, his privacy under surveillance and his experience of racism, and what work changes would help?

consultant_note.history: Dr. King, 36, is seen at the request of Dr. Ashby-Nwankwo. For about two months, after a winter of continuous campaigning and an admission for exhaustion six months ago, he has had low mood most days, loss of pleasure in reading and preaching, guilt that he cannot do more, poor concentration, fatigue and broken sleep of about five hours, with an hour to fall asleep and waking before five. His energy returns on the platform but drains afterwards. He has lived for nearly ten years with threats against his life and his family, including the bombing of his home, a stabbing that required chest surgery, jailings, and anonymous threats, one of which urged him to take his own life; he believes his calls are monitored. He is watchful in crowds and at home, but has no nightmares, flashbacks, avoidance or emotional numbing. He has never had a period of elevated mood, high energy or little need for sleep. At twelve, grieving his grandmother, he impulsively injured himself; he has not had thoughts of suicide since and has none now. He speaks calmly of the likelihood that he will be killed. His faith, his family and his congregation sustain him. He fears that a psychiatric record could be used against him and his work
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Ashby-Nwankwo's intake note and tests: PHQ-9 17 with item 9 scored 0, GAD-7 11, PC-PTSD-5 2, AUDIT-C 2; blood count, metabolic panel, TSH and hemoglobin A1c normal; ECG normal with QTc 412 ms. assessment.assessment: He has five or more DSM-5-TR symptoms, including depressed mood and loss of interest, for more than two weeks, with impairment, so this is major depression and not an adjustment disorder, which cannot be diagnosed when the criteria for another disorder are met. Severity is moderate. There is no history of hypomania and the MDQ is negative, so an antidepressant is appropriate. Threat, surveillance, racism and overwork are causes of the episode, not personal failings, and are recorded as psychosocial factors

He was exposed to traumatic events, but he has no intrusion or avoidance symptoms, and his vigilance is proportionate to a real and continuing danger. PTSD criteria are not met; PC-PTSD-5 2 agrees. Screening should be repeated, because symptoms can emerge later

No current suicidal ideation, intent, plan or preparatory behavior. The impulsive act in childhood grief, the letter urging suicide, depression and insomnia raise risk; his faith, purpose, family, congregation and engagement in care are strong protective factors. His expectation of being killed is a realistic appraisal of danger, not passive suicidal ideation, and should be distinguished from it at each review. Overall risk is low; outpatient care with the safety plan is appropriate

Insomnia on most nights for more than three months with daytime impairment, driven by late-night work, travel and hyperarousal. Sleep apnea is unlikely. CBT for insomnia is the first-line treatment; a hypnotic is not advised

Stopping smoking does not worsen depression and often improves mood. In the EAGLES trial varenicline did not significantly increase serious neuropsychiatric events in smokers with psychiatric disorders, and it was the most effective option. Starting it a few weeks after sertraline lets side effects be told apart

recommendations: Weekly cognitive behavioral therapy with behavioral activation and CBT for insomnia, with a therapist of his choosing who will work with his faith; then every two weeks once he responds, and monthly in remission
Sertraline 25 mg each morning for a week, then 50 mg; tolerability check by telephone two weeks after starting; increase only if the PHQ-9 has not fallen by about eight to twelve weeks
CBT for insomnia: fixed rising time, a sleep window widened as sleep improves, no work in bed, no tobacco or coffee in the evening; no hypnotic
PHQ-9 at every visit; suicide risk reassessed at every visit, distinguishing expectation of being killed from a wish to die; PC-PTSD-5 again at about three months
Varenicline with counseling, starting about three weeks after sertraline, with a quit date a week later and mood watched
A sustainable work plan: a full day off each week, no more than two speeches a day, delegation of travel and correspondence, and a two-week break in the summer
Privacy: restricted chart, documentation limited to what care requires, and secure video for follow-up
Psychiatry review by video at about eight to twelve weeks, sooner if needed
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Ashby-Nwankwo, who saw him the same day. The diagnosis, the reasons PTSD is not diagnosed, the safety assessment and the options were explained to Dr. King, who chose therapy and sertraline and agreed to the work plan
